articles.fullText:
As the evening cools, people begin heading outside. Couples walk through their neighborhoods. Parents take children to nearby parks. Older residents stroll together, while others walk alone, taking a few laps around a familiar route.
It can look like exercise, but it doesn't always feel like it. For many people, the evening walk is simply part of what happens after dinner.
Why walk after dinner?
There is a familiar Chinese saying: 饭后百步走，活到九十九 — "Walk 100 steps after a meal and live to 99."
The "100 steps" is not meant to be taken literally. Rather, the saying reflects a long-standing belief that gentle movement after eating is good for the body. Some Chinese health guidance has traditionally linked a slow post-meal walk with digestion, while warning against strenuous exercise immediately after eating.
Traditional Chinese medicine also offers an explanation for the practice, linking gentle movement with the health of the digestive system. Beijing's Traditional Chinese medicine authorities have described slow walking after a meal as a way of supporting digestion, while emphasizing that "walking 100 steps" means gentle movement rather than vigorous exercise.
People stroll and stretch along a walkway at Beijing Olympic Forest Park during an evening walk. 
Modern research offers some support for the broader idea.
A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis looked at eight randomized controlled trials involving 116 people and found that exercise after eating reduced post-meal blood glucose more than exercising before a meal or remaining inactive. The researchers also found that the timing of exercise mattered, with activity closer to the meal producing a greater effect. The authors cautioned, however, that the included trials had a high risk of bias and the sample was small.
A Chinese health expert has made a similar distinction. At a 2025 National Health Commission press conference, Peking Union Medical College Hospital physician Li Jingnan said moderate walking after a meal can promote intestinal movement and may help with post-meal fullness or reduced gastrointestinal motility. But strenuous exercise after eating can instead place additional stress on the digestive system.
So the old saying is not really an instruction to exercise after every meal. It is closer to an invitation to keep moving gently rather than immediately sitting or lying down.
And that may help explain why the habit has lasted.
A public square transforms into a community gathering space as local residents join an evening dance routine after dinner. 
Walking as social time
For many people, an evening walk is also an opportunity to spend time with other people.
A friend can be invited along. Parents can take their children outside. Couples can use the time to talk after a busy day.
Research has increasingly looked at the relationship between physical activity and social connection. The World Health Organization notes that walking is an accessible form of physical activity that can be incorporated into recreation and everyday life.
That social element is particularly visible in China's parks. An evening walk can easily turn into an evening gathering.
In some places, people dance. In others, they practice tai chi, play badminton, use outdoor fitness equipment or simply sit and chat.
The activity may change, but the principle is similar: people have a reason to leave their homes and spend some time outside.
A resident walks his dogs through a neighborhood park, reflecting the relaxed rhythm of post-dinner strolls in China. 
From health habit to social ritual
This is what makes the after-dinner walk interesting. The health explanation may be one reason people walk, but it doesn't fully explain the atmosphere that develops around it.
A walk gives people somewhere to go after dinner without requiring a particular destination.
It can be a chance to talk with a partner, accompany a child, meet a friend or simply spend some time outdoors before returning home.
In that sense, the walk sits somewhere between exercise and leisure. It is movement without the pressure of a workout.
That distinction matters in a city like Beijing, where public space can change character throughout the day. Parks, residential compounds, sidewalks and riverside paths can become informal gathering places as temperatures drop and people finish eating.
The city slows down, but it doesn't stop.
A neighborhood playground fills with families at dusk, offering children a chance to play and unwind after dinner. 
A different kind of exercise
As someone who runs regularly, I notice the difference immediately.
Running usually comes with a purpose. There is a distance to cover, a pace to maintain or a route to complete. Even an easy run can feel like a workout.
Walking after dinner doesn't have to.
You can stop to talk. You can change direction. You can walk slowly. You can turn around after 10 minutes because you've had enough.
There is something appealing about movement that asks so little of you.
And perhaps that is part of why the habit fits so naturally into everyday life. It doesn't require special equipment, a gym membership or a large block of time. Dinner is already happening. The walk simply comes next.
In Traditional Chinese Medicine, slow walking after a meal supports digestion by promoting gentle movement without straining the body. 
An ordinary part of the evening
There is a tendency to think of fitness in terms of deliberate effort: running a race, joining a gym, following a training plan or tracking a personal best.
The evening walk is almost the opposite. It is unremarkable.
That may be exactly why it works.
In China, a walk after dinner can be a health habit, a family routine, a chance to catch up with a friend or simply an excuse to get out of the house.
It doesn't need to be labelled. It doesn't need to be measured.
And it doesn't need to be particularly long.
As the evening stretches on and people gradually make their way home, the paths become quieter again. Tomorrow, many of them will do it all over again.
Dinner. Then a walk.
Editor's Note: Denique Daniëls is a multimedia editor for CGTN Digital. This article is part of China in Motion, a recurring column that explores contemporary Chinese life through movement – from running and walking to the design of public space, health culture and community. By observing cities at a human pace, the series captures how ordinary routines shape the experience of life in China.

articles.summaryCn: 中国首条国家级规划建设的江海联运运河平陆运河正式通航，大幅缩短西南地区出海距离并降低物流成本，同时在建设过程中注重生态保护与野生动物通道建设。

paragraphs.en:
The Pinglu Canal in south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region officially opened to {{0}} {{1}} on Wednesday, marking the country's first major river-to-sea canal project planned and {{2}} at the national level since 1949. The 134.2-kilometer waterway connects the Xijiang River {{3}} with the Beibu Gulf, cutting the {{4}} shipping distance between southwestern China and the sea by more than 560 kilometers. articles.fullText:
The Pinglu Canal in south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region officially opened to commercial navigation on Wednesday, marking the country's first major river-to-sea canal project planned and coordinated at the national level since 1949.
The 134.2-kilometer waterway connects the Xijiang River corridor with the Beibu Gulf, cutting the traditional shipping distance between southwestern China and the sea by more than 560 kilometers.
A view of Pinglu Canal in south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region. 
A new gateway for China-ASEAN trade
For decades, much of the cargo from China's southwest had to travel eastward before reaching the sea through Guangdong and other coastal areas. The Pinglu Canal provides a more direct route to the Beibu Gulf, allowing vessels of up to 5,000 tonnes to sail from the inland river network to the sea.
Local authorities estimate that the shortcut could reduce logistics costs by 18% to 30%, saving about 5.2 billion yuan ($720 million) each year.
The canal also forms a key part of the New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor, giving inland regions such as Chongqing, Chengdu, Guizhou and Yunnan a more direct maritime gateway to Southeast Asia.
The timing is significant. China and ASEAN have been each other's largest trading partners for six consecutive years. In the first half of 2026, their trade reached 4.34 trillion yuan, up 18.2% year on year.
The Beibu Gulf is already becoming an important gateway for that trade, with container throughput at Beibu Gulf Port reaching about 10 million TEUs in 2025, compared with around 2.28 million TEUs in 2017.
The canal could further expand the port's economic hinterland, allowing manufactured goods to move south toward ASEAN markets and agricultural products, minerals and other raw materials to move north into China's inland economy.
But connecting economies also means cutting through landscape. For Pinglu Canal, that has meant designing infrastructure not only for ships, but also for the species and ecosystems along its route.
Longmen Bridge near the estuary of Pinglu Canal in Qinzhou, Guangxi, August 25, 2026. 
Building a canal while keeping nature connected
At the Qingnian navigation hub, engineers built a dedicated fish passage to help aquatic species overcome a water-level difference of nearly 10 meters.
The passage is more than 480 meters long and contains 120 pools. By gradually reducing water levels and flow velocity, the system allows fish to move upstream step by step. A separate passage has been designed for eels and other species capable of crawling or climbing.
Monitoring equipment has been operating since 2025. Project monitoring data show that more than 10 fish species have used the passage, with about 76,000 upstream movements and 115,000 downstream movements recorded.
On land, a similar principle is being applied.
At the Fenshuiling section, a wildlife-only bridge crosses the canal. Covered with soil and native vegetation, the overpass reconnects forest habitats separated by the waterway. It is designed to allow species including leopard cats, masked palm civets and red-bellied squirrels to cross what would otherwise be a physical barrier.
The measure follows recommendations from a 2025 study published in the journal Land, which assessed habitat fragmentation across 11 regional wildlife groups and called for dedicated ecological corridors to be incorporated into infrastructure planning.
The project's environmental approach also extends to the enormous amount of material generated during construction.
Engineers excavated roughly 315 million cubic meters of earth and rock. More than 98% of the material was reused for riverbank reinforcement, soil remediation and the creation of about 13,900 mu, or 927 hectares, of farmland.
The opening of the canal marks the beginning of another phase. As commercial traffic grows, maintaining water quality, preserving wildlife movement and protecting coastal ecosystems will require continuous monitoring and management.
Estuary of Pinglu Canal in the Maowei Sea waters of Qinzhou, Guangxi, August 25, 2026. 
The Pinglu Canal is intended to create new connections — between inland China and the sea, between China and ASEAN, and between production centers and global markets. The challenge now is to ensure that these new connections do not permanently disconnect the ecosystems along its route.

Business confidence among US companies in China rebounded sharply amid stronger financial performance, a more stable geopolitical landscape and perceived regulatory progress, according to AmCham Shanghai's 2026 China Business Report, released on September 10.
Of the 262 member companies surveyed, 78% said their China businesses were profitable in 2025, while 58% were optimistic about their five-year outlook in China.
Industrial robots transport components for inspection at a smart workshop in Yueqing, Zhejiang Province, China, September 8, 2026. 
The rebound in business confidence was accompanied by stronger investment activity. A total of 28% of respondents increased their investment in China in 2025, the highest share in four years. Views of the business environment also improved, with 55% describing it as transparent, up seven percentage points from a year earlier.
Eric Zheng, president of AmCham Shanghai, emphasized the great importance of the Chinese market, mainly from two dimensions.
China remains one of the most efficient manufacturing bases in the world and continues to be a highly strategic market for members' products and services, Zheng said. "That underpins the positive sentiment," he added.
Among members with US operations, three-quarters confirmed that their China presence benefits their US operations in some way, with one-third emphasizing that their China presence enhances the global competitiveness of their US operations.
A notable strategic shift is also emerging, with more surveyed companies adopting a global-oriented strategy. The "in China for the world" strategy has become the top business priority for 29% of surveyed companies in 2026, surpassing the "in China for China" model chosen by 24%.
ABB Robotics showcases its robotics and automation solutions at productronica China 2026 in Shanghai, China, March 26, 2026. 
More respondents are also betting on China-based innovation, the report said. Half of surveyed members with China-based research and development (R&D) facilities plan to increase R&D spending this year, up sharply from one-third in 2025.
In a vote of confidence in the Chinese market, General Motors (GM) in August announced a 20-year extension of its joint venture partnership with Chinese automaker SAIC Motor, with it now running to 2047.
"We will continue to strengthen our performance here in China by developing products and technologies in China, for China, and bringing them to market faster," said John Roth, senior vice president of GM and president of GM China. The joint venture plans to launch at least 30 new energy vehicle models by 2030.
"We see meaningful opportunities to grow beyond China. SAIC-GM has strong local capabilities across engineering, manufacturing and quality, and we can apply those strengths in select international markets, including the Middle East, Africa, South America, Mexico and Asia-Pacific," Roth said.
The front of the Siemens booth is seen at the Shanghai New Expo Center during the World Artificial Intelligence Conference 2026 in Shanghai, China. July 20, 2026. 
Siemens offers another example. Its Digital Native Factory in Nanjing, the German technology group's largest research and production center for computer numerical control systems, drives and electric motors outside Germany, was added to the World Economic Forum's Global Lighthouse Network in January.
The factory has introduced digital twins, modular automation and more than 50 AI applications. Siemens said these technologies had cut its time to market by one-third compared with 2022.
In a March interview with Xinhua, Siemens global executive vice president Xiao Song said the breadth of China's industries, the depth of its manufacturing system, the speed of technological innovation and the openness to new technologies created opportunities for foreign companies.
A separate 2026 survey by the European Union Chamber of Commerce in China also identified innovation, cost and speed as strengths of the Chinese market. However, it noted continuing economic pressure, market access barriers and regulatory concerns.
Jeffrey Lehman, chair of AmCham Shanghai, said members had seen improvements in the regulatory environment, reinforced by steadier China-US relations. He also called for a stable and transparent framework that supports cross-border trade and investment.

The opening ceremony of the 2026 Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Forum on Traditional Medicine was held on Thursday in Nanchang, Jiangxi Province, bringing new opportunities for the growth and international cooperation of traditional medicine.
This year's event set a record for international attendance, drawing 81 delegates from 21 countries, including Sri Lanka, Belarus, India and Kazakhstan. The delegation features senior government officials, health ministers, foreign diplomats and representatives from international bodies such as the SCO Secretariat and the World Federation of Chinese Medicine Societies. Officials noted that the strong participation of high-level leaders signals a shift in traditional medicine cooperation – moving from basic academic exchange toward joint platform building and shared institutional mechanisms.
The 2026 Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Forum on Traditional Medicine takes place in Nanchang City, east China's Jiangxi Province, September 17, 2026. 
A major highlight of the forum is its focus on technological innovation and practical application. A special release session for new policies, standards, technologies and products will unveil cutting-edge sector achievements, such as AI-assisted diagnostic tools and intelligent herbal processing systems. Spanning policy dialogues, standard mutual recognition and product commercialization, the forum aims to serve as a primary launchpad for innovation and global product debuts in traditional medicine.
Addressing the ceremony, Yin Hong, secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Jiangxi Provincial Committee and chairman of the Standing Committee of the Jiangxi Provincial People's Congress, highlighted Jiangxi's progress in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), noting that the sector reached 27.9 billion yuan (about $3.93 billion) in revenue. With 3,146 TCM institutions across the province, Jiangxi has built a "15-minute TCM healthcare service circle," ensuring accessible, high-quality care for residents.
The opening ceremony of the 2026 Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Forum on Traditional Medicine in Nanchang City, east China's Jiangxi Province, September 17, 2026. 
Yin emphasized that as the SCO marks its 25th anniversary, recent SCO initiatives prioritizing AI and the digital economy have injected fresh momentum into traditional medicine. Jiangxi will leverage digital technologies to build smart TCM service systems, develop AI-assisted diagnostics and utilize the SCO multilingual platform to make quality healthcare more accessible globally.
Shen Yueyue, vice-chairperson of the National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC) and chairperson of the Good-Neighborliness, Friendship and Cooperation Commission of the SCO (GNFCC SCO), noted that since its launch in 2020, the forum has held five sessions, forging a path of cooperation that aligns with both the principles of traditional medicine and the shared needs of regional countries.
"The forum serves as an essential platform for policy dialogue, yielding key consensuses such as the Nanchang Initiative and the Nanchang Consensus to deepen regional collaboration," Shen said.

Beyond high-level policy dialogues and technological showcases, the event features parallel sessions designed to strengthen international education standards and build cross-regional industrial supply chains, alongside interactive exhibitions showcasing traditional medical history and digital healthcare tools like thermal moxibustion robots. Delegates will also participate in field visits across Jiangxi to inspect key research laboratories, leading pharmaceutical companies and major medical institutions.
The three-day event, held from September 16 to 18, focuses on integrating smart technologies with traditional medicine expertise to enhance global public health. The forum is co-hosted by the People's Government of Jiangxi Province and the GNFCC SCO.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and members of her reshuffled Cabinet arrive at the prime minister’s office in Tokyo on September 17, 2026. 
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi reshuffled her cabinet on Thursday, retaining most key ministers while bringing in a newcomer from the Japan Innovation Party (JIP), the junior coalition partner of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP).
It is Takaichi's first cabinet reshuffle since she took office last October.
According to the new lineup, Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara, Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi, Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi and Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama all remained in their respective posts.
Among those entering the cabinet for the first time, House of Representatives members Kazuo Yana and Yoshihiro Seki had previously been disciplined by the LDP over a high-profile political slush fund scandal. They were named agriculture minister and education minister, respectively. This marked the first time since the scandal came to light that lawmakers disciplined by the party over the affair had received cabinet positions.
Hiroshi Nakatsuka, formerly secretary general of the JIP, was appointed minister in charge of regulatory reform, making him the first JIP member to serve as a cabinet minister. The move marked a shift from the LDP and JIP cooperating outside the cabinet to cooperation within the cabinet.
Shigeaki Koga, a former official at Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, said that on foreign and security policies, the JIP is even more hawkish than Takaichi and could potentially encourage the prime minister to pursue more hawkish policies.
Another focus of the reshuffle is the absence of former Internal Affairs and Communications Minister Yoshimasa Hayashi from the new cabinet. Hayashi was Takaichi's rival in last year's LDP presidential election.
Analysts said the personnel changes indicate, on the one hand, that the Takaichi administration will press ahead with its established military buildup, proactive fiscal policy, and diplomatic agenda.
The Takaichi government is set to revise Japan's three key security documents by the end of this year, potentially including plans to acquire large numbers of unmanned systems and move toward mass production of hypersonic missiles.
On the other hand, Takaichi's latest cabinet reshuffle is also aimed at consolidating her administration's power base and paving the way for her to secure another term as LDP president in next autumn's party leadership race.
